newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN CAR SECTOR SLAMS NEW TAXES, TO DEMONSTRATE.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN CAR SECTOR SLAMS NEW TAXES, TO DEMONSTRATE.

text.p: The Belgian car sector on Friday slammed the government's decision to raise excise duties on petrol and called a demonstration for October 27.
"Too much is too much," Ingmar Jonkers, chairman of the Belgian federation of car and motorcycle manufacturers (FEBIAC), said in a statement.

The Belgian government said early this month excise duties on petrol would rise two francs per litre as part of its 1997 budget which aims to cut the public deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997 to comply with Europe's single currency rules.
The new taxes should yield 7.26 billion francs. In addition, the government will start charging social security contributions for company cars, a measure it valued at four billion francs.
"The comparison between car drivers and lemons being squeezed further with each new budget is not a coincidence," Jonkers said. For many people, their car is not a luxury but a vital tool, he said.
He said the new tax rises were the 12th since April 1992. Car drivers now pay 300 billion francs per year in taxes -- one seventh of the government's total fiscal income.
"Every 1,000 francs (petrol) fill up means a 740 franc present to the state," Jonkers said.

He said the October 27 demonstration through the centre of Brussels -- backed by garage, petrol distribution, vehicle assistance and car dealer associations -- would show the government that car drivers were fed up.
He added the car sector was not opposed to fiscal measures but that these should help improve road safety, mobility and environment.
"(The Belgian government's) fiscal policy excels by its lack of creativity and vision," he said.
Ford Motor Company (Belgium) NV, , the Belgian car importing and distributing unit of U.S. Ford Inc , said the new taxes increased pressure on the car sector.
"People will become even more cautious and refrain from investing in new cars," spokesman Wilfried Baeken said.
"It will lead to a price war, because everyone will want to keep their market share, their share of the pie," he said.
He said sales would drop by the end of the year.
But D'Ieteren , which imports and distributes Volkswagen (VW), Audi, Porsche, Seat and Skoda cars, said the taxes would not have a significant impact on sales in the short term.
"The price of diesel remains unchanged and we have a solid position in this market segment, a spokeswoman said. Diesel vehicles account for 60 percent of D'Ieteren's sales, she said.
"But nevertheless, the car sector is still the milk cow of the government," she said.
